A 4-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department due to ongoing vomiting and complaints of
abdominal pain. Her parents found her in this condition after being cared for by a babysitter. She has
no prior medical history. Family history includes depression, suicide, neuropathic pain, diabetes,
hypertension, cancer, and angina. On arrival, the child is minimally responsive and confused. Her vital
signs are as follows: temperature 100.9°F (37.8°C), blood pressure 118/75 mmHg, pulse 153/min,
respirations 23/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Examination reveals a confused child
actively vomiting bloody material into a basin. Laboratory results are as follows: - Serum: - Na+: 140
mEq/L - Cl-: 101 mEq/L - K+: 3.9 mEq/L - HCO3-: 11 mEq/L - BUN: 20 mg/dL - Glucose: 99 mg/dL -
Creatinine: 1.0 mg/dL Abdominal radiography demonstrates several radiopaque objects in the
stomach. Urine and serum toxicology results are pending. Which of the following is the most likely
cause of her intoxication? Answer Choices: (A) Mercury (B) Nortriptyline (C) Lithium (D) Zinc (E)
Calcium carbonate (F) Iron (G) Lead (H) Aspirin (I) Acetaminophen (J) Bismuth subsalicylate
 A. Zinc
B. Calcium carbonate
C. Lead
D. Mercury
E. Aspirin

F. Lithium
G. Bismuth subsalicylate
H. Nortriptyline
I. Acetaminophen
J. Iron
